title: What You Can Customize on a Drinkware Order | EVERCUP
description: Colour, finish, logo method, lid and components, packing — what can be changed on an existing model, how each decoration method behaves, and where the minimum order changes.

blocks.lead: Customization is not one decision. Colour, surface, logo method, lid, components and packing each carry their own minimum, cost and risk — and one of them usually decides whether the project is viable at your quantity.
blocks.image_alt: Injection moulding equipment in the factory workshop
blocks.caption: Decoration is planned before moulding — the surface a part needs depends on what happens to it next.

blocks.h2: Four layers of customization, from cheapest to deepest.
blocks.intro: Buyers often ask for everything at once. The order below is the order in which cost rises — and the order in which each layer changes what the next one can do.

items.title: Colour and surface
items.text: Match a Pantone on the body, or choose from the standard colour chips. Gloss, frosted, matte or soft-touch. A custom colour needs a run of its own — 250 pieces is the practical floor, and the chip has to be approved under the light it will be seen in.
items.meta: From 250 pcs for a matched colour

items.title: Logo and artwork
items.text: Screen print, UV print, heat transfer, laser or hydro dip. One colour of print is a different project from a full wrap: colour count, print area, curvature and the surface under the ink all change the price.
items.meta: From 10 pcs · one to eight colours

items.title: Lid and components
items.text: Swap to another lid in the library, add a straw, plug, coaster or sleeve. A component we already tool is a configuration change; a component that does not exist is a new mould.

items.title: Packing and presentation
items.text: Poly bag, white box, printed sleeve, gift box, insert, hangtag or barcode. Packing is where a promotional cup becomes a retail product, and it carries its own minimums.

blocks.h2: Five ways to put a logo on a cup.
blocks.intro: The right method is decided by the artwork, the surface, the quantity and how long the product has to look good. This is the short version; each method has its own page with the details.

blocks.note: Every method above is confirmed on a physical sample. A screen proof tells you the file is right; only a decorated sample tells you the cup is right.

blocks.h2: Why the same cup has three different minimums.
blocks.intro: The minimum is not a policy — it is what the setup costs. A print screen, a colour match and a mould are three completely different investments.

head: What you change
Typical minimum
Why
rows: Existing model, plain or one-colour print
No setup beyond the screen; the model already runs
Multi-colour print or a full wrap
Each colour is a pass; setup has to be absorbed
The press runs a dedicated colour batch
Custom lid or component on an existing body
One new mould, but a small one
2–4 mould sets have to be paid for
blocks.note: Where a buyer needs fewer pieces than the minimum, the honest options are: pick a different configuration, accept a higher unit price for a short run, or pay the setup separately. We quote all three when asked.

items: Can I mix designs in one order to reach the minimum?

Yes on print — several artwork versions can share one production run if the model and colour are the same. They cannot share a tooling investment, so a mixed order does not unlock a lower MOQ on a new mould.
Can you match a Pantone colour exactly?

We match to a chip you approve under an agreed light source. Plastic, ink and coating each render a colour slightly differently, so an exact match across body and print is confirmed on a sample, not on a screen.
Silicone is a different surface and needs its own validation — pad printing or laser rather than a standard screen pass. Ask before you build artwork around it.
Can artwork be changed after the sample is approved?
Yes, before the press starts. After that, the change is a new run — which is why the approval email is treated as the production reference.
